case.dispatchHook: Fort Myers nursery logs say an orange tree grew pine cones. It did not.
briefing: Agent, a plant nursery outside Fort Myers just scrambled its growth records.
The log says a zebra longwing left its chrysalis as an egg. It says an orange tree grew pine cones.
Put the butterfly's life cycle back in order, then sort out the plant files.
The nursery would like its records to make sense again. So would I.

lab.intro: The growth log for one zebra longwing came back shuffled. Put each stage back where it belongs.
lab.prompt: Put the stages of the zebra longwing's life cycle in order, starting with the egg.

steps.name: Egg
steps.card: A tiny yellow dot laid on a passionflower leaf

steps.name: Caterpillar
steps.card: Eats leaves and grows, shedding its skin as it gets bigger

steps.name: Chrysalis
steps.card: Hangs still in a hard case while its body changes

steps.name: Adult butterfly
steps.card: Has wings, flies, and lays eggs to start the cycle again

lab.why: A butterfly goes through complete metamorphosis: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, then adult, and the adult lays new eggs.

case.debriefClosed: Case closed. The nursery logs match the plants again, and the butterflies are back in order. Log it.
case.debriefOpen: Case stays open for now. It comes back as a cold case soon, and the plants will still be growing.

items.stem: A strong storm blows across a field near Fort Myers. A sunflower bends in the wind, but it stays in the ground. It also keeps getting water from the wet soil. Which plant part does both of these jobs?
options: leaf
root
flower
fruit
why: Decoy: leaves make food using light, but they do not hold the plant in the soil.
Correct: roots hold the plant in the ground and take in water from the soil.
Decoy: the flower makes seeds, and it does not take in water from the soil.
Decoy: fruit holds and protects seeds, but it does not anchor the plant.
keyWords: getting water from the wet soil
items.alt: A flowering plant with its root, stem, leaves, flower, and fruit labeled.
items.tisCheck: Root functions only (holding the plant and taking in water); SC.3.L.14.1 limits are UNVERIFIED, so the item uses plain part names and jobs with no tissue terms.
items.misconceptions: Leaves take in rain water; flowers drink water for the plant; fruit is only food for people.

items.stem: Kai puts the cut stem of a white daisy into a cup of water mixed with blue food coloring. He checks the petals each day and records what he sees. What does this investigation show about the stem?
options: The stem makes food for the flower using light.
The stem holds the seeds until they are ready.
The stem takes in blue color from the air.
The stem carries water up to other parts of the plant.
why: Decoy: the leaves, not the stem, are the main place a plant makes food using light.
Decoy: seeds form in the flower and are held in the fruit, not in the stem.
Decoy: the blue came from the water in the cup, not from the air.
Correct: the blue water moved up through the stem to the petals, so the stem carries water.
items.alt: A table of petal color by day: day 1 white, day 2 white with light blue edges, day 3 blue streaks on every petal.
items.tisCheck: Stem function (carrying water) only; SC.3.L.14.1 limits are UNVERIFIED, so no tissue names and no computation.
items.misconceptions: Stems make the plant's food; seeds are stored in stems; color or water enters a plant from the air.

items.stem: A live oak and a gopher tortoise both live in a sandy Florida field. Both need food for energy. Which statement correctly describes how each one gets food?
options: The live oak makes its own food in its leaves using light. The tortoise eats plants.
The live oak and the tortoise both make their own food using light.
The live oak takes in its food from the soil through its roots. The tortoise eats plants.
The live oak and the tortoise both take in their food from the soil.
why: Correct: plants such as the live oak make their own food in their leaves using light, and animals such as the tortoise must eat.
Decoy: a tortoise warms up in sunlight, but it cannot make its own food the way a plant can.
Decoy: roots take in water and nutrients, but the plant's food is made in the leaves.
Decoy: neither one gets food from the soil, because the oak makes its food and the tortoise eats plants.

captions: Gopher tortoise: eats grasses and leaves

items.alt: A gopher tortoise standing on sandy ground.
items.tisCheck: Leaves make food using light and plants make their own food while animals cannot (SC.3.L.14.1 scope); no photosynthesis vocabulary or chemical terms.
items.misconceptions: Plants get their food from the soil; animals that bask in the sun make food like plants.

items.stem: Ms. Reyes set up two bean seedlings for one week. Pot 1 stood upright in a room with light coming only from a window on the left. Pot 2 was laid on its side in a dark closet. The table shows what happened. Which statement best explains both results?
options: Stems grow toward warm air, and roots grow toward wet soil.
Stems grow down with gravity, and roots grow up toward light.
Stems grow toward light and upward, and roots grow down with gravity.
Both seedlings bent because they were too heavy to stand up straight.
why: Decoy: the results match light and gravity, and nothing in the setup tested warm air or wet soil.
Decoy: this is backward, because the stems grew toward the window and up while the roots grew down.
Correct: the stem in Pot 1 bent toward the light, and in Pot 2 the stem turned up while the roots turned down with gravity.
Decoy: the seedlings bent in a set direction, toward light and away from gravity, not because of their weight.
keyWords: light coming only from a window on the left
laid on its side in a dark closet

visual.title: Bean Seedlings After One Week
rows: The stem bent toward the window.
On its side in a dark closet
The stem turned to grow up. The roots turned to grow down.

items.alt: A table showing that the stem in Pot 1 bent toward the window, and that in Pot 2 the stem turned up and the roots turned down.
items.tisCheck: Plant responses to light and gravity (SC.3.L.14.2, also assessed with SC.3.L.14.1); no tropism vocabulary, and limits are UNVERIFIED so the scenario stays plain.
items.misconceptions: Plants grow toward heat or water only; stems and roots respond the same way; plants droop from weight.

items.stem: Ava collected seeds from four plants that grow in Florida. She wrote down what each seed looks like. Which seed is most likely carried to new places by sticking to an animal's fur?
options: coconut
dandelion
Spanish needle
beautyberry
why: Decoy: a coconut's husk is full of air, so it floats on water to new beaches.
Decoy: a dandelion seed has a fluffy top, so the wind carries it.
Correct: tiny hooks catch on fur and socks, so animals carry Spanish needle seeds to new places.
Decoy: beautyberry seeds sit inside berries that birds eat and drop somewhere else.

visual.title: Ava's Seed Notes
rows: Large seed inside a thick husk full of air
Tiny, with a fluffy top like a parachute
Thin and dark, with two tiny hooks on one end
Small, inside a soft purple berry

items.alt: A table describing four seeds: coconut, dandelion, Spanish needle, and beautyberry.
items.tisCheck: Seed dispersal by water, wind, and animals (SC.4.L.16.1, also assessed with SC.3.L.14.1); Florida plants, no plant classification.
items.misconceptions: All seeds travel by wind; any seed eaten by an animal is the one that sticks to fur.

items.stem: A farmer near Fort Myers grows watermelons. He covers some flowers with mesh bags that let in light, air, and water but keep bees out. He leaves other flowers uncovered. Which statement best explains the results in the table?
options: Bees carry pollen between flowers, and the flowers need pollen to make fruit and seeds.
The bags blocked the light, so the covered flowers could not make food.
Bees bring water to the flowers, so the covered flowers dried out.
Fruit grows from the roots, so the flowers did not matter.
why: Correct: without bees, pollen did not reach the covered flowers, so they could not make fruit and seeds.
Decoy: the stem says the bags let in light, and flowers are not where a plant makes most of its food.
Decoy: the bags let water in, and bees carry pollen, not water.
Decoy: fruit grows from the flower, which is why the covered flowers made almost no melons.
keyWords: let in light, air, and water

visual.title: Watermelon Flowers
rows: Most grew into melons with seeds.
Most dried up and fell off.

items.alt: A table: uncovered watermelon flowers that bees could visit grew into melons with seeds; covered flowers dried up and fell off.
items.tisCheck: Pollination as the step that lets a flower make fruit and seeds (SC.4.L.16.1, also assessed with SC.3.L.14.1); no fertilization details or flower part names.
items.misconceptions: Bees feed or water flowers; fruit forms from roots or leaves; any covering blocks light.

items.stem: The zebra longwing is Florida's state butterfly. The diagram shows its life cycle, but one stage is not named. Which stage belongs in the spot with the question mark?
options: nymph
chrysalis
tadpole
young butterfly with small wings
why: Decoy: a nymph is the young stage of insects like grasshoppers, which have no resting stage.
Correct: after the caterpillar stage, a butterfly forms a chrysalis, and the adult comes out of it.
Decoy: a tadpole is the young stage of a frog, not a butterfly.
Decoy: butterflies do not grow from small-winged young, because their wings form inside the chrysalis.
items.alt: A ring of four life cycle stages with arrows: an egg on a leaf, a caterpillar, a stage marked with a question mark, and an adult butterfly.
items.tisCheck: Stages of complete metamorphosis in a Florida butterfly (SC.4.L.16.4, PARTIAL limit: Florida plants and animals only).
items.misconceptions: Butterflies have a nymph stage; tadpole used for any young animal; wings grow a little at a time.

items.stem: An eastern lubber grasshopper and a zebra longwing butterfly both hatch from eggs in Florida. How is the grasshopper's life cycle different from the butterfly's?
options: The young grasshopper looks like a small adult without wings, and it has no chrysalis stage.
The grasshopper also rests inside a chrysalis before it becomes an adult.
The young grasshopper looks like a worm and has no legs.
The grasshopper goes from egg straight to adult, with no young stage.
why: Correct: a grasshopper goes through incomplete metamorphosis, so its young look like small adults and there is no resting stage.
Decoy: only insects with complete metamorphosis, like butterflies, have a resting stage such as a chrysalis.
Decoy: this describes the young of some insects with complete metamorphosis, not a grasshopper.
Decoy: a grasshopper has a young stage, the nymph, which grows and sheds its skin before it becomes an adult.
keyWords: How is the grasshopper's life cycle different
items.alt: A ring of four stages with arrows: grasshopper eggs, a small nymph, a larger nymph, and an adult grasshopper.
items.tisCheck: Complete vs incomplete metamorphosis with Florida insects (SC.4.L.16.4, PARTIAL limit: Florida plants and animals only); no molting details.
items.misconceptions: All insects form a chrysalis; insect young are always wormlike; some insects skip the young stage.

items.stem: A class kept a log of four insects found around their Florida school. Which insect goes through complete metamorphosis?
options: green darner dragonfly
eastern lubber grasshopper
lady beetle
palmetto bug
why: Decoy: young dragonflies live in water and look different, but they have no resting stage, so this is incomplete metamorphosis.
Decoy: young grasshoppers look like small adults and never rest, so this is incomplete metamorphosis.
Correct: the young look nothing like the adult and there is a resting stage, which means complete metamorphosis.
Decoy: young palmetto bugs look like small adults with no wings, so this is incomplete metamorphosis.

visual.title: Insect Growth Log
rows: Lives underwater in a pond, six legs, no wings
A small adult with no wings
A tiny, spiky worm with legs, not like the adult
Yes, stays still on a leaf while its body changes
A small adult with no wings

items.alt: A table of four insects showing what each one's young look like and whether it has a resting stage.
items.tisCheck: Complete vs incomplete metamorphosis judged from described stages, Florida insects only (SC.4.L.16.4, PARTIAL); no stage vocabulary required beyond the benchmark.
items.misconceptions: Any young that look different from the adult means complete metamorphosis; water-living young are a resting stage.

items.stem: A slash pine and an orange tree both grow in Florida. Both make seeds. Use the table to compare them. Which statement correctly groups the two plants?
options: Both are flowering plants, because both make seeds.
The orange tree is a nonflowering plant, and the slash pine is a flowering plant.
The slash pine is not a seed plant, because it has no fruit.
The orange tree is a flowering seed plant, and the slash pine is a nonflowering seed plant.
why: Decoy: making seeds does not make a plant a flowering plant, because pines make seeds without flowers.
Decoy: this is backward, because the orange tree has flowers and the pine does not.
Decoy: a pine is a seed plant, and its seeds form on cones instead of inside fruit.
Correct: the orange tree makes flowers and fruit with seeds, while the pine makes seeds on cones with no flowers.
items.alt: A table: the orange tree makes flowers and its seeds form inside fruit; the slash pine makes no flowers and its seeds form on cones.
items.tisCheck: Flowering vs nonflowering seed plants with Florida trees (SC.4.L.16.4, PARTIAL limit: Florida plants and animals only); seeds and cones only, no spores.
items.misconceptions: Every seed plant has flowers; a plant without fruit is not a seed plant; cones are a kind of flower.

items.stem: A green tree frog lays its eggs in a pond in Florida. Which list shows the stages of its life cycle in order?
options: tadpole, egg, tadpole with legs, adult frog
egg, adult frog, tadpole, tadpole with legs
egg, tadpole with legs, tadpole, adult frog
egg, tadpole, tadpole with legs, adult frog
why: Decoy: the life cycle starts with the egg, and a tadpole hatches from it.
Decoy: the adult frog is the last stage, not the second.
Decoy: a tadpole grows legs as it changes, so the tadpole without legs comes first.
Correct: a tadpole hatches from the egg, grows legs, and then becomes an adult frog.
keyWords: lays its eggs in a pond
stages of its life cycle in order
items.alt: An adult green tree frog with smooth green skin.
items.tisCheck: Stages in the life cycle of a Florida frog (SC.4.L.16.4, PARTIAL limit: Florida animals only); no gill or lung changes required.
items.misconceptions: The tadpole comes before the egg; legs appear at hatching; a frog hatches as a small adult.

items.stem: A student wrote four cards about the life cycle of a live oak, a flowering tree. The cards are out of order. Starting with the acorn in the soil, which order is correct?
options: W, X, Y, Z
W, Y, X, Z
Y, W, Z, X
W, Y, Z, X
why: Decoy: pollen moves between the flowers of a grown tree, so a seedling must grow first.
Correct: the acorn sprouts, the seedling grows leaves, the grown tree's flowers get pollen, and then it makes new acorns.
Decoy: a seedling grows from a sprouted acorn, so the sprouting card comes first.
Decoy: a tree makes acorns only after its flowers get pollen, so card X comes before card Z.

visual.title: Live Oak Cards
rows: An acorn in moist soil takes in water and sprouts a root.
Wind carries pollen between the grown tree's flowers.
A seedling grows its first leaves.
The tree makes new acorns, each holding a seed.

items.alt: A table of four cards, W to Z, each describing one stage in the life of a live oak.
items.tisCheck: Major stages of a Florida flowering seed plant, including germination and pollination (SC.4.L.16.4, PARTIAL limit: Florida plants only); no fertilization details.
items.misconceptions: Trees make seeds without flowers; pollination happens in seedlings; the life cycle starts with a small plant, not a seed.
